questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: name the main idea of a short passage rather than a detail of it
questions.stem: A paragraph reads: 'Durante veinte años, el mercado del pueblo funcionó solo los jueves y cerró los domingos por la tarde. Cuando se abrió la tienda grande junto a la carretera, el mercado amplió su horario a los siete días y muchos puestos adelantaron el cierre al mediodía. Hoy abre tres días, pero cada vez menos gente llega temprano.' Which sentence states that paragraph's main idea?

options.text: Lengthening the hours of a market that once traded on one day has not brought back the early crowds
A village market was closed for good as soon as a large shop opened beside the road
options.misconception: reads a shortening of hours as a permanent closure of the market

options.text: Traders on a market square would rather finish work at midday than in the afternoon
options.misconception: turns one habit of the traders into the subject the passage never adopts

options.text: The arrival of one large shop made every other shop in the county keep longer hours
options.misconception: spreads the effect of a single shop across a whole county the text ignores

questions.explanation: A main idea is the claim every sentence serves, and here the three sentences move from one day of trade, to a widening of hours, to fewer early arrivals, so the figure the paragraph is really about is the mismatch between longer opening and thinner crowds. The other three answers each pick up a piece and drop the point: one says the market closed, which the last sentence denies; one promotes a habit of the traders to the subject, which it never is; and one generalises a single shop's effect across a county, which the passage nowhere claims.
questions.hint: Ask what every sentence in the paragraph is doing for the same claim.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: separate a stated detail from the inferences a reader is tempted to add
questions.stem: A short notice reads, 'El ferry sale de la dársena norte a las ocho y media y el acceso a pie se cierra quince minutos antes.' Which detail does the notice actually establish?

options.text: Someone on foot has to finish the walk to the boarding point a quarter of an hour before eight thirty
The boarding gate is shut permanently at eight thirty and cannot be opened again afterwards
options.misconception: turns the closing of a walking access into a permanent shutting of the gate

options.text: The crossing itself lasts a quarter of an hour once the vessel has left the quay
options.misconception: moves the quarter of an hour from the access to the journey across the water

options.text: A driver may park beside the north quay right up until the moment the vessel sails
options.misconception: extends a rule about walkers into a permission for drivers the notice never gives

questions.explanation: The notice names two times and one is earlier than the other, and all that follows from that arithmetic is that a walker must set out so as to arrive fifteen minutes before the eight thirty departure. It says nothing about the gate staying shut, nothing about the length of the crossing, and nothing about parking, so each of those answers supplies a fact the text withholds. Reading for detail means taking the words as far as they will go and no further, and the habit that keeps a reader honest is asking which words in the text produce the claim.
questions.hint: Ask which two times the notice gives, and what follows from their order.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: identify a tone from the choices a writer makes rather than from the subject
questions.stem: A notice opens, 'Quisiera detenerme un momento en algo que nos afecta de cerca. Nadie ha dicho nada, y por eso precisamente conviene decirlo ahora. No es una queja; es una cuenta.' What tone does the writer adopt in those three sentences?

options.text: Controlled urgency, since each sentence narrows the point and refuses the comfort of vagueness
Open anger, since the accusation is aimed at people who have said nothing whatever
options.misconception: reads a deliberately measured opening as an outburst at unnamed people

options.text: Light irony, since the repeated negation marks amusement at how long the delay has run
options.misconception: takes a repeated negation as a mark of amusement rather than of insistence

options.text: Formal distance, since the conditional politeness removes the writer from the matter
options.misconception: reads a conditional opening as withdrawal when the next sentences close in

questions.explanation: Tone is a matter of choices rather than of subject matter, and the choices here are a conditional opening, a narrowing of the audience to those close to the matter, an explicit refusal of the word complaint, and a closing image of an account rather than an outburst. A writer who was angry would not stop three times to delimit the case, and a writer being ironic would leave the reader to work out which party is at fault rather than naming the point. The politeness of quisiera is not distance either, because the sentence immediately closes that distance by saying it affects everyone closely.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer refuses to call the thing, and why that refusal matters.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an attitude towards a subject from the mood of a passage
questions.stem: A column says, 'Probablemente el ayuntamiento no tiene dinero para la biblioteca y probablemente no lo tendrá. Aun así, la biblioteca necesita una azotea y lo tendrá.' What is the writer's attitude towards the council?

options.text: Impatience with the excuses, and confidence that the building will be answered for anyway
Sympathy with the council, since the writer accepts its financial position as the last word
options.misconception: takes the repeated concession of a difficulty as agreement with the party that has it

options.text: Indifference, since the writer reports two probabilities and declines to choose between them
options.misconception: believes a writer who states an outcome is refusing to take a side

options.text: Hostility to the library, since the writer treats the claim of the library as the unreasonable one
options.misconception: reverses the target of the column by reversing which side is doubted

questions.explanation: An attitude is a position taken towards a party, and the position here is set by the shape of the paragraph: the council's difficulty is conceded twice and then dismissed in a single short clause, so the writer is not weighing the arguments but declining them. Sympathy would leave the second probablemente standing as the last word, and indifference would not insist on an outcome. The hostility reading reverses the target, since the sentence that ends the column is a statement of what the library will get, which is not the language of a writer trying to discredit it.
questions.hint: Ask which clause the writer spends least time on, and what that does to it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: identify an author's stated purpose in an opening the reader wrote
questions.stem: Your own opening paragraph reads, 'En las dos páginas siguientes explico por qué se retrasó el proyecto, qué se hizo durante el retraso y qué puede aprenderse de él el próximo equipo.' What work is that paragraph doing?

options.text: It names the three things the text will do, so the reader knows the route before any evidence
It proves that the delay was avoidable, so the paragraphs that follow serve only as illustration
options.misconception: reads a list of promised explanations as if the case were already closed

options.text: It establishes the writer's standing in the matter, which the argument then depends on
options.misconception: reads a promise about the text as a claim about the writer's credentials

options.text: It announces a conclusion, so the paragraphs between it and the end become the proof
options.misconception: takes a route map to be a position the rest of the text must defend

questions.explanation: A first paragraph that lists what a text will do is a route map, and its purpose is to let a reader follow rather than to persuade, which is why it can be checked against the headings that follow. The answer that says the delay was already proved there is wrong because the paragraph contains no evidence at all, only three promises. Establishing standing would need a sentence about the writer's role or knowledge, and a conclusion would commit the text to a position, whereas explicar here only promises an explanation.
questions.hint: Ask whether the paragraph contains a claim to defend or a plan to follow.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A thesis in an original passage
questions.learningObjective: find the thesis of a passage the reader wrote from the last line
questions.stem: A passage reads: 'Cada año se pierde cerca de la quinta parte del agua que capta la ciudad y buena parte se escapa por fugas bajo la calle que nadie mide. Repararlas costaría menos que ampliar la planta y además no gastaría agua nueva. Escribo estas líneas para pedir que se empiece por medir.' Which sentence is the thesis of that passage?

options.text: Measuring the leaks should come first, because repair is both cheaper and would not spend new water
The city loses a fifth of its water each year and the figure has not moved in ten years
options.misconception: adds a claim about the stability of the figure that the passage never makes

options.text: Enlarging the treatment plant is the cheapest way to guarantee a supply for the coming decade
options.misconception: reverses the preference of a passage that argues for repairing leaks first

options.text: Water is lost under the streets, so households that use most of it ought to be charged more
options.misconception: supplies a remedy of charging households that the passage never proposes

questions.explanation: A thesis is the position the rest of the passage serves, and here the writer gives a loss, a comparison of costs, a second advantage of repair, and then says outright what the lines are asking for, so measuring first is the position and the rest is support. The figure in the first sentence is evidence rather than a position, and a thesis has to be something a reader could disagree with, which a measurement is not. The other two answers reverse the preference of the passage: it argues against enlarging the plant, and it never proposes charging households at all.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence the writer could be argued against, and which ones support it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: label the parts of an argument and the move between them
questions.stem: An argument runs: a claim that the school needs a second hall; a count of how many pupils now sit in one room; the council's reply that its budget is fixed for the year; and a second point that the same building was used as a store until 1975. What structure is that?

options.text: A claim, supporting evidence, an answer to it, and a point that makes the answer harder to accept
A conclusion, the reasons behind it, a sentence to introduce the topic, and two examples
options.misconception: reorders the argument into a shape that puts its conclusion at the front

options.text: Two positions given equal weight and no preference expressed between them at any point
options.misconception: stops reading at the council's reply and misses the sentence that turns it

options.text: A definition of the problem, an anecdote, a quotation, and a repetition of the definition
options.misconception: reads a fact about the building's old use as material of a different kind

questions.explanation: The sequence can be labelled by asking what each sentence does to the one before it: the first commits the writer to a need, the second makes that need measurable, the third is the reply that arrives from outside, and the fourth turns the reply back against itself by showing the building was once used for something cheaper to run. That last move is what makes this an argument rather than a report, because it accepts the reply and then shows the reply does not settle the case. An even-handed presentation would have ended at the third sentence, since nothing after it favours a side.
questions.hint: Ask what each sentence does to the reply, and whether anything favours a side.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Bias and the evidence for it
questions.learningObjective: infer a writer's bias from the parties a sentence names and the parties it leaves out
questions.stem: A piece opens, 'Los vecinos de este barrio llevan treinta años tolerando el ruido de la discoteca del centro.' What does that opening reveal, and what in it is the evidence?

options.text: It treats the dispute as the neighbourhood's problem, though only the discotheque is described as noisy
It treats the dispute as the discotheque's problem, though only the neighbours are described as noisy
options.misconception: swaps the grammatical subject and object of the sentence to reverse its lean

options.text: It assumes nothing about fault, because the sentence names two parties and then stops
options.misconception: takes the naming of two parties to be a neutrality the syntax does not give

options.text: It assumes the noise is acceptable, because tolerar is used in place of a complaint
options.misconception: reads a verb describing endurance as a verdict that nothing is wrong

questions.explanation: Bias shows up in what a sentence is built to hold still, and this sentence is built so that the neighbours are the subject and the discotheque is the object, with tolerar doing the work of a verb the other side would have used differently. The evidence is grammatical rather than stated: the party who acts is the one described as putting up with something, and the party acted upon is the one whose conduct is described without comment. A reader who wants the bias of a text should look first at which noun the sentence makes the subject, since that is the choice hardest to make by accident.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two parties the sentence makes the subject and which it makes the object.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A claim the evidence does not support
questions.learningObjective: identify the gap between a figure cited and the conclusion drawn from it
questions.stem: A short report states that the town's two libraries between them lend four thousand books a year, and concludes, 'The reading habits of the town are declining.' What is wrong with that conclusion?

options.text: The lending figure measures use of the libraries, not the reading of people who never visit them
The figure is too small to indicate anything, since four thousand volumes cannot be counted
options.misconception: dismisses a figure on the grounds of size instead of on the mismatch of subject

options.text: A decline can never be read from one year's figure, so the number itself must have been wrong
options.misconception: concludes that a figure is false rather than that a conclusion outruns it

options.text: Lending is a service measure, so no conclusion of any kind may be drawn from it at all
options.misconception: overcorrects a mismatched conclusion into a ban on any conclusion whatever

questions.explanation: The number and the conclusion do not describe the same population: the figure counts books that passed through two library counters, and the conclusion is about how a whole town reads, including the people who own their books, borrow elsewhere or read nothing. An argument that generalises from a service to a whole population has changed the subject in the middle, and that is a gap no amount of arithmetic can close. The other answers each overcorrect: a number can certainly indicate something, one year can support a limited comparison, and a service measure supports claims about that service.
questions.hint: Ask who is counted by the figure, and who the conclusion is about.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Inference that follows and one that does not
questions.learningObjective: separate what a passage carries from what a reader adds
questions.stem: A passage says, 'El puente se cerró en enero y no volvió a abrirse hasta mayo. Durante esos cuatro meses el ferry atendió el mismo recorrido con dos salidas diarias.' Three of the four statements below follow from the passage and one does not. Which three?

options.text: For four months the ferry was carrying traffic that had previously crossed by road
Without the ferry, that route would have had no crossing of any kind in the same period
The bridge was shut for every part of the four months the passage describes
The ferry service was withdrawn as soon as the bridge reopened at the start of May
options.misconception: treats the end of a passage's account as a statement about what happened next

questions.explanation: An inference has to be carried by something in the text, and three of these are: the ferry is said to attend the same route, which implies the traffic that the bridge had carried; the route has one crossing described and one substituted, which leaves no crossing if the substitute is removed; and no opening between January and May is reported, so the bridge was shut throughout. The fourth statement goes past the passage, which says the ferry was running during those four months and stops there, and a text that ends at the moment the bridge reopens says nothing whatever about the service afterwards. Absence of a mention is not a mention of an absence.
questions.hint: Ask which of the four can be read out of the two sentences without adding anything.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Purpose in an opening the writer composed
questions.learningObjective: read an opening that withdraws a reader's expectation as a statement of purpose
questions.stem: Your own opening paragraph reads, 'Este informe no propone una solución; explica por qué la propuesta anterior no funcionó.' What does that paragraph do to a reader's expectations?

options.text: It withdraws the expectation of a proposal, so the rest is read as an explanation rather than a plan
It promises a solution and then withdraws it later, once the reasons for the failure have been given
options.misconception: inserts a promise the opening never makes before the refusal

options.text: It puts the conclusion first, so the paragraphs that follow are the working out of a settled case
options.misconception: reads a statement of scope as a position the rest of the text defends

options.text: It excuses the writer from having to argue, because a negative opening closes off discussion
options.misconception: believes refusing to propose relieves a writer of the duty to argue

questions.explanation: An opening that says what a text will not do is doing something more useful than it looks, because it removes the wrong frame before a reader can settle into it. Having been told there will be no proposal, a reader approaches the reasons as the real subject and does not spend the first page looking for a recommendation. The paragraph is not promising and then withdrawing, because nothing in it promises a solution first, and it is not a conclusion, because no position has been taken. What it does is state the purpose negatively, which is a legitimate way to be direct about scope without spending the opening on the writer's own plan.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would look for, and whether the paragraph has told them it is not there.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Comparing two passages on one theme
questions.learningObjective: identify what changes between two treatments of the same subject
questions.stem: You have written two passages of ninety words each on the closing of a village shop, one for a notice on the door and one for a report to the county. Which difference between them matters most?

options.text: The notice can count on people who were there, while the report has to supply the chain of causes
The notice may leave out every detail, while the report must include every detail the writer knows
options.misconception: assumes an official text has to carry the whole of what the writer knows

options.text: The notice is written in the past tense, while the report must be written in the present tense
options.misconception: makes the tense a requirement of genre rather than of the events described

options.text: The report may be the shorter text, since official documents are read more quickly than notices
options.misconception: assumes official documents are read faster than a notice on a shop door

questions.explanation: The two texts share a subject and a length but not a reader, and the reader is what forces the difference: someone posting a notice on the door they used to shop in needs the address, the date and the reason in three lines, while a reader in the county has never been in the shop and needs the sequence, since a name alone does not explain why a bus route or a supermarket changed the trade. Neither text is a shorter version of the other, and neither is a more formal one, because the difference lies in what has to be supplied rather than in the register. A writer who reuses a notice as a report produces a document its reader cannot use.
questions.hint: Ask what each reader already knows, and what each reader has to be told.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: compress a notice without changing what it says
questions.stem: A notice reads: 'El puente de la carretera vieja lleva cerrado desde enero. Mientras dure la reparación, el ferry hace dos salidas diarias, una a las siete y otra a las trece. El tránsito de camiones pesados queda prohibido por el puente y debe pasar por la carretera alta, que añade dieciocho kilómetros. El ayuntamiento calcula que las obras terminarán en octubre.' Which sentence is an accurate summary of that notice?

options.text: A closed bridge is being crossed by ferry twice a day while heavy lorries take a longer inland road
The ferry service will keep running twice a day until the repair works are finished in October
options.misconception: turns a description of what is happening into a promise about what will happen

options.text: Lorry traffic has been banned throughout the county until the bridge reopens at the end of October
options.misconception: enlarges a ban on one bridge into a ban across a whole county

options.text: The county has added eighteen kilometres of new road in order to serve the ferry terminal itself
options.misconception: reverses which of the two places the extra kilometres are meant to reach

questions.explanation: A summary keeps the shape of the original, so it has to carry the closed bridge, the substitute crossing and the diversion for heavy vehicles, and the first of these four sentences carries exactly those three. The second turns a description of what is happening into a prediction about what will happen, which adds a commitment the notice never makes, and the third enlarges a ban on one bridge into a ban across a county. questions.hint: Ask which of the four statements keeps every relation between the facts intact.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A paragraph with one controlling idea
questions.learningObjective: judge whether a paragraph's evidence reaches its controlling idea
questions.stem: A paragraph begins, 'El uso de la bicicleta en la ciudad ha caído un doce por ciento en dos años, y la causa no parece ser el precio del combustible.' The rest gives the same figure for three neighbouring towns, the results of a survey of forty drivers, and a note that the city's cycle lanes end at the ring road. What does that paragraph have, and what does it lack?

options.text: One controlling idea and evidence that reaches it, since each item bears on the fall in cycling
Two competing controlling ideas, since the fuel price and the missing lanes argue against each other
options.misconception: mistakes two factors being weighed for two positions being defended

options.text: One controlling idea and no evidence for it, since the figures and the survey are about other towns
options.misconception: dismisses comparison with other towns as though it were about a different subject

options.text: No controlling idea, since a paragraph about a fall in cycling must state the price of fuel
options.misconception: insists the paragraph state a fact its first sentence explicitly sets aside

questions.explanation: A paragraph is sound when every sentence after the first is reachable from it, and here the opening commits the writer to a fall and a rejection of the obvious explanation, and the three items that follow each do work on that: comparable figures show the fall is not a local accident, the survey tests the fuel-price explanation, and the note about the lanes offers the factor the survey cannot see. The second answer makes a conflict out of two things that are being weighed, and the third treats comparison across towns as though the paragraph were about the towns. What a paragraph needs is not one kind of sentence but one question that each sentence helps to answer.
questions.hint: Ask what question the opening sentence asks, and whether each later sentence helps answer it.

questions.topic: A transition that names the relation
questions.learningObjective: read a transition as a statement about the logic joining two sentences
questions.stem: A paragraph ends, 'La tasa de absenteeismo bajó un cinco por ciento.' The next sentence begins, 'Ese descenso no se explica por la climatización, instalada en 2019.' What is that opening doing?

Repeating the first sentence in other words, so that the point of the paragraph is driven home

options.text: Introducing a new subject, so the second sentence can be read on its own without the first
options.misconception: claims independence where the second sentence takes its subject from the first

options.text: Putting the cause before the effect, so that the reader meets the explanation before the fact
options.misconception: reverses the order of the two sentences as the paragraph gives it

Ese descenso makes the link explicit and sin embargo turns it into opposition, so a reader cannot mistake the first sentence for an argument for the second. The answer that calls it a repetition is wrong because the two sentences say different things, and the answer that calls it a new subject is wrong because the subject of the second is the descent named in the first.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: screen candidate thesis statements against the demands a thesis must meet
questions.stem: A writer's opening sentence is being checked before the essay is drafted. Three of the following are demands a working thesis statement must meet. Which three?

options.text: It takes a position a reasonable reader could disagree with
It is narrow enough to be argued for in the space the writer actually has
It repeats the wording of the question the writer was set
options.misconception: treats a restated question as though a question could serve as a position

options.text: It fixes a scope in time or place instead of claiming to cover everything at once

questions.explanation: A thesis is a job description for the rest of the essay, and three of these say what the job involves. It has to be arguable, or nothing follows from it because nobody could disagree; it has to be small enough that the writer can actually reach it, since a claim about a whole century cannot be earned in two thousand words; and it has to fix a scope, because a claim with no boundary can be met by any evidence at all. questions.learningObjective: tell a conclusion that carries new weight from one that restates the argument
questions.stem: A five-paragraph essay has argued that a town's library should open on Saturdays. Which closing sentence adds something rather than restating?

The town should therefore open its library on Saturdays, as this essay has argued throughout
options.misconception: repeats the claim in the language the introduction already used

options.text: In conclusion, the case for Saturday opening has been made and the council should now decide
options.misconception: announces that the essay is over instead of giving the reader a reason

options.text: Libraries, as we all know, are the heart of a community and must not be allowed to fade away
options.misconception: substitutes a general sentiment for anything said anywhere in the text

questions.topic: Claim and support in an original argument
questions.learningObjective: state the claim an argument supports and the support it actually gives
questions.stem: A short piece reads: 'El registro de la piscina municipal anota dos mil entradas en un mes de invierno, y la misma piscina cerró ocho días por una avería del calentamiento. The pool should close for the winter, because two thousand entries do not justify the running cost

options.text: The pool is run badly, since eight days lost in one month show the heating cannot be relied on
options.misconception: turns a problem the piece reports into a verdict on the management

options.text: The council has already chosen to repair, since the figure of two hundred thousand euros is given

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: explain what a translator must carry across that a word-by-word rendering drops
questions.stem: Explain what a Spanish translator has to preserve when rendering the English sentence 'I would be grateful if you could send the figures by Friday', and say why a close word-for-word version fails.

It carries the register, which is a formal and deferential one, so the Spanish has to open at a distance: le agradecería que me enviara las cifras antes del viernes, or se lo agradecería if the writer wishes to be warmer without losing the deference. And it carries a deadline expressed as a preference, which is why antes del viernes works where el viernes is wrong. A word-for-word version fails because it keeps the first person pronoun and the modal in a way that reads flat, and because it produces enviar las cifras as a flat request with no sign that the writer is unwilling to insist. The test a translator can apply is to ask what the sentence would be doing to the relationship if it were said aloud in Spanish, because a phrase that is polite in one language can sound curt in another and a phrase that is curt in one can sound insolent in the other.

The English sentence is deferential without being weak, and a Spanish rendering that uses the imperative or that drops the conditional has changed the social act even though every content word is still present. The converse error is as common, since a Spanish sentence that would be perfectly polite in a shop can be stiff in a letter, and a translator who matches the word will hand the reader a tone the writer never chose. It helps to treat register as a second meaning alongside the first: a phrase has to be right for the situation, and the situation includes who is writing to whom and how much each of them is willing to be pushed.

What stays is often the modesty that the impression was hiding: many and can be are weak words that make a sentence checkable, while very and extremely make a strong sentence that nobody can test. questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: explain a procedure for checking whether a conclusion follows from the evidence offered
questions.stem: Explain to a learner how to test whether a conclusion in a short report actually follows from the evidence the report offers, and name two failures that pass unnoticed.

answer.exemplar: The test is to write the conclusion as a sentence with a blank where the evidence goes, and then see whether the report can fill the blank without adding anything. A short report says the town's two libraries lend four thousand volumes a year and concludes that reading habits are declining; the blank is that four thousand volumes, and the report cannot fill it with a fact about habits, because the figure describes people who went in and says nothing about the people who did not. Two failures pass unnoticed in this kind of writing. The first is the change of subject, where a measure of a service is quietly used as a measure of a population, and the second is the change of tense, where a figure for one year is read as a direction of travel without a second year to compare. A third, the commonest of all, is a cause claimed out of an association: two things rise together in every district, and the report chooses one of them as the cause without holding the other fixed. None of the three is repaired by a longer sentence, which is why the blank is the quickest check available: it is a question about what the text contains, and a text that cannot answer it is short of evidence no matter how confident its tone.

questions.explanation: Learners are usually shown how to summarise a report and how to judge its tone, and neither of those skills tells them whether the last sentence is supported. The reason a conclusion can be wrong while every sentence above it is accurate is that a conclusion is a new claim, and a new claim needs evidence of its own. The procedure of writing the conclusion with a blank in it forces the question of what would have to be true, which is the same question a sceptical reader will ask, and it makes the failure visible before the paragraph is finished rather than after it is printed. The two failures worth naming for a learner are the change of subject, from a service to a population, and the change of period, from one figure to a trend, because both produce sentences that sound reasonable and are supported by nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be in the report for the last sentence to be supported.

It has to keep the dates, since a notice about works with no dates in it tells a reader nothing they can plan around, and it has to keep the condition, since sin no hay lluvia is what makes March a plan rather than a promise. What may go is the name of the road, the identity of the contractor and anything about the traffic arrangements, because a one-sentence summary has no room for detail that does not change what a reader would do. questions.explanation: The two stages fail in different ways, and a learner who is asked only for the first will produce a fluent sentence that has quietly changed the notice. A summary is judged on two counts at once, which one is short and which is faithful, and the second is the one that is hard to see because the sentence still contains the words of the notice. Hedges are the part that goes first, since a conditional or a proviso reads as clutter to a writer in a hurry, and they are also the part that carries the difference between what is planned and what is certain. A writer who can be made to say what may be dropped will also find that the dates, the amounts and the conditions are never the things to drop.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would do differently if the summary left the condition out.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: explain what happens to an idiom in translation and what can be done about it
questions.stem: Explain to a learner what happens to an English idiom when it is translated word for word into Spanish, and say what a translator has to decide before choosing a Spanish expression.

answer.exemplar: A word-for-word rendering of an English idiom produces a sentence that is grammatical in Spanish and means nothing there, because the idiom works in English by an association of images that Spanish does not share. Take the English idiom to bite the bullet: a literal Spanish version would be morder la bala, and a Spanish reader hears a joke about an animal chewing ammunition rather than a statement about doing something unpleasant. What the translator has to decide is whether the English idiom carries a meaning, a tone, or both, and a decision follows from that: if the meaning matters, the idiom has to be replaced with a Spanish expression that says the same thing, and if the tone matters, the image has to be kept and the surroundings adapted so that it still lands. Neither choice is free, because a Spanish expression that carries the meaning may be flatter than the English, and a Spanish image that carries the tone may not fit the situation. The test a translator can apply is to say the Spanish version aloud to somebody who has never heard the English, and to ask whether they would understand it as a picture or as a claim.

questions.explanation: Idioms are the part of a text that a learner is most likely to translate badly and a reader is most likely to misunderstand, and the reason is that the idiom looks like ordinary words. A translator who is thinking about words will be right about the words and wrong about the sentence, and the mistake is invisible until somebody acts on it. The decision about meaning or tone is worth teaching because it changes what a translator looks for: a meaning-led translator hunts for an equivalent, and a tone-led translator hunts for a Spanish image that fits the company the other words keep. A learner who has been told that idioms do not translate has been given half the lesson, since some of them can be carried across nearly intact and the rest cannot be carried at all.
questions.hint: Ask what a Spanish reader would picture in the literal version, and whether that picture is the one the English meant.

questions.topic: Finding a thesis that is never stated
questions.learningObjective: explain how to recover a thesis a passage argues rather than announces
questions.stem: Explain to a learner how to find the thesis of a passage that never states it in a single sentence, and say what evidence settles the answer.

answer.exemplar: The method is to write down what the passage is doing, sentence by sentence, and then ask which single claim would make all of those actions sensible. A passage that reports more trees planted each spring, fewer each autumn, a contractor paid on last year's budget and two neighbours who say the square looks unchanged is not reporting four facts, and the claim that makes all four sensible at once is that the planting depends on money that arrives too late to be judged. The evidence that settles it is that a thesis of this kind must reach the last sentence as well as the first, and the two candidates usually fail in different ways: one covers the first half and leaves the neighbours stranded, and the other covers the neighbours and turns the budget into a detail. Two tests are worth giving a learner. A thesis must be something a reader could disagree with, which rules out a summary of the figures, and it must be the one claim on which the sentences would be in the wrong order if it were false, which is how a writer can find an argument that is being made without being announced.

questions.explanation: Some passages argue rather than assert, and a learner who is trained to look for a thesis sentence will find none and conclude that the passage has no argument. The claim is usually there, and it is there in the arrangement: passages argue through the order of their sentences and through the pattern of their concessions, so a writer who compares the figures and the objection and the budget can often name the claim that the writer never put in a sentence of its own. The failure that matters is naming a summary instead, because a summary is a list of what the passage said and it cannot be disagreed with, and a passage whose thesis is a summary has nothing to argue. Teaching the two tests, arguable and order-dependent, gives a learner a way to check an answer that no amount of reading will supply.
questions.hint: Ask what the passage would look like if one particular claim turned out to be false.

options.misconception: believes a thesis may not begin as a statement of fact

questions.explanation: A thesis has to be arguable and it has to have an edge, and this sentence fails both: no reader can disagree with a claim that libraries matter, and a claim about libraries in general has no boundary an essay could cross. The two failures are related, since a statement that cannot be disagreed with is usually one whose scope has never been narrowed. The other three answers each name something that is not a problem here, since a thesis need not echo the question, length is not one of the three criteria, and a thesis may begin as a statement of fact provided a writer then argues for it. The test a learner can apply is to put the sentence in front of somebody who wants to disagree and see whether they have anything to say.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader could disagree, and whether the sentence fixes a boundary.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: read a text's purpose from the paragraph it ends with
questions.stem: A short report runs for four paragraphs of figures and closes, 'Por eso pedimos que la comisión aplaza la votación hasta que haya un estudio de costes.' What does the closing paragraph tell you about the whole report?

options.text: That the report exists to obtain a delay, so the figures are the argument for a request
That the report exists to inform, so the figures are the whole of what it has to give
options.misconception: ignores a request the closing paragraph makes in terms

options.text: That the report is a criticism of the commission, so its purpose is to damage its reputation
options.misconception: turns a disagreement about timing into an attack on a body

options.text: That the report was commissioned to produce a study, so its purpose is to write one
options.misconception: reverses cause and effect between a study and a request for one

questions.explanation: A report's purpose is often declared in its last paragraph, because that is where the writer says what the earlier paragraphs were for, and here the closing sentence asks for a delay, which tells a reader that the four paragraphs of figures are an argument rather than a description. The second reading takes a description of the state of play for the whole purpose, which ignores a request the text makes explicitly. The third reads a disagreement about timing as an attack on a body's reputation, and the fourth reverses cause and effect, since a study is requested rather than delivered. The practical habit is to read the last paragraph first, because it is usually the shortest statement of what the rest is doing.
questions.hint: Ask what the report asks for at the end, and what that makes the figures for.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A literary period named by its dates
questions.learningObjective: read what a period label asserts about when a body of writing belongs together
questions.stem: A history of Spanish literature has a section headed 'La generación de 1925'. What is that heading doing?

options.text: Grouping writers who began publishing about the same date, so the label is a marker of a moment and not a style
Describing a shared style, so the label commits the writers to a manner of writing that never varied
options.misconception: believes a date in a period label stands for a uniform style

options.text: Naming a single event, so the label says that something particular happened to the writers in 1925
options.misconception: turns a year of publication into an event that befell the writers

options.text: Rejecting any connection between the writers, so each is presented as a case entirely on his own
options.misconception: contradicts the purpose of grouping writers under one heading

questions.explanation: A label built from a year is a way of grouping writers by when they came to public notice, and it makes a claim about a moment rather than about a manner, so a reader should expect shared concerns and not shared sentences. The second reading is the mistake every literary history warns against, since writers brought together by a date usually differ in style and often argue with each other. The third reading turns a date of publication into an event that happened to the writers, and the fourth contradicts the purpose of grouping them at all. Knowing that a period is named by a date is also what lets a reader handle the overlaps, because the same writer appears in more than one such group.
questions.hint: Ask whether the year in a label points at a moment of publication or at a style of writing.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a comparison a writer has to set out
questions.stem: Five steps of a short comparison have been listed out of order. Which sequence is the order in which a comparison is normally written?

options.text: What is being compared and why the comparison is worth making at all
The two terms of the comparison set out with their features in the same order
The point at which the two terms agree, so the comparison is not a rigged one
The point at which they differ, stated with the feature rather than in general terms
What follows from the difference, and what a reader should now do about it

questions.explanation: A comparison has a fixed order because the parts do not take the same weight. It opens by saying what is being compared, since a reader who does not know the two terms cannot follow anything, and then the terms are set out in the same order so that the features line up. The point of agreement comes before the point of difference, and that is not politeness: a comparison that opens with a difference and never returns to an agreement reads as an attack, and a reader who has been given nothing in common has no reason to trust the comparison of what differs. The difference is then stated in terms of the feature rather than in general, and the paragraph closes on what follows from it. Putting the conclusion before the features is the tempting order and it is the one that makes a comparison useless.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader needs before each of the following steps can be understood.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: explain how a translation can be accurate in words and wrong in register
questions.stem: Explain to a learner how a translation can be accurate in its words and still get the register wrong, and say what a translator checks to prevent it.

answer.exemplar: A translation can be word-perfect and still sound wrong, because register is not carried by the words but by the relationship the sentence sets up, and a sentence that is polite in English can be curt in Spanish while an ordinary Spanish sentence can be too warm for an English letter. Take the English instruction please note that the room must be ready by eight. Rendered as por favor, anota que la sala debe estar lista a las ocho, every content word is right and the sentence is unremarkable, except that por favor in a note to a colleague who has been asked to do this before reads as either a reproach or a stranger's politeness. What the English please is doing is softening a demand, and the softening has to be done again in Spanish, this time with a construction that fits the relationship: le agradecería que la sala estuviera lista a las ocho, or simplyifying the demand in a way the writer has some right to use. The check a translator can apply is to ask who is entitled to say this to whom, because that question is about the relationship and the words will follow from the answer.

questions.explanation: Learners who translate for meaning alone are usually right about the content and wrong about the social act, and the mistake shows up first with the small words that carry politeness and informality, since those are the ones with the most alternatives in any language. Please, just, actually, quite and by the way all have a Spanish counterpart that is not interchangeable with the others, and choosing the wrong one changes how a reader hears the sentence without changing what it says. A second source of mismatch is the pronoun, since a Spanish version that uses usted where the English had no pronoun at all can sound stiff, and one that uses tú where the English was formal can sound careless. Testing the register is a matter of asking about the relationship, not about the words, and it is the one check a learner rarely does.
questions.hint: Ask who is entitled to say this to whom, and whether the words fit that relationship.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A controlling idea and the sentence that drifts
questions.learningObjective: name a paragraph's controlling idea and the sentence that stops serving it
questions.stem: Stage one: state the controlling idea of the paragraph that opens, 'La biblioteca del barrio cierra a las ocho, y a las nueve ya no queda nadie dentro.' Stage two: name the sentence that no longer serves it.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the controlling idea is that the neighbourhood library is not being used in the evening, which is a claim about how the building is treated rather than about its opening hours. Stage two: the sentence that drifts is any one that turns to a fact about the building itself, such as a note that the roof was repaired in 2019, because a repair says nothing about whether anybody comes in after eight and cannot be reached from the claim. The test for the second stage is to ask what question the drifting sentence helps to answer, and if the answer is not the question the opening sentence asked, the sentence belongs in another paragraph. A paragraph of this kind often drifts towards a fact it knows better, and the repair is exactly that: a real and interesting fact that has nothing to do with the point being made, which is why a writer who notices the drift can cut it without losing anything.

questions.explanation: The two stages fail in different ways, and the second is the one a writer finds hard, because a drifting sentence is usually true and usually interesting, and nothing in it is wrong. Controlling ideas are easy to state and easy to lose, since a paragraph can begin well and then pick up a fact that belongs to another paragraph, and the loss is invisible in a single reading because each sentence reads well on its own. The test given in the second stage is the one that catches it, since a sentence either helps answer the question the opening sentence asked or it does not, and there is no third case. A writer who applies that test to every sentence will find at most one or two drifters in a paragraph, and cutting them usually makes the paragraph stronger rather than shorter.
questions.hint: Ask what question the drifting sentence helps to answer, and whether it is the one the opening sentence asked.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.learningObjective: choose the features that belong to a formal written register in Spanish
questions.stem: A letter from a firm to a supplier reads, 'Nos dirigimos a ustedes para solicitarles una cotización actualizada de los trabajos previstos. Quedamos a la espera de su respuesta antes del día 20.' Three of the features below belong to a register of this kind. Which three?

options.text: A plural pronoun of address together with the matching plural verb form
A noun in the third person standing in for the people doing the writing
An opening particle such as oye used to draw the reader into the sentence
options.misconception: lists a mark of a familiar spoken register as a mark of a formal one

options.text: A sentence that ends with a tag placed after the final comma, as in vale, no?
options.misconception: lists a mark of a familiar spoken register as a mark of a formal one

options.text: A form for the future of obligation, in which the request is made about a settled arrangement

questions.explanation: A formal business register is built out of choices that keep the writer at a distance, and three of these are exactly that. The plural pronoun with the matching plural verb keeps the addressee in a role rather than in a conversation, the third person noun stands in for the people signing the letter so that no individual has to be answerable, and a form of future obligation states a settled arrangement instead of a wish. The other two are the marks of a familiar spoken register, and they are conspicuous in a letter precisely because a letter has no use for them. A learner who writes these two into an email to a supplier will not be misunderstood, and the message will still arrive, but the message will read as a note passed to a colleague rather than as an offer of work.
questions.hint: Ask of each feature whether it puts the writer at a distance from the reader or draws the reader in.
